title: Price a feeder failure

blocks.text: A distribution company prices the failure of each feeder before it ranks renewals. A failure interrupts every customer on the feeder. Crews then switch a share `switch_share` of them to a neighbouring feeder after `switch_hours`; the rest wait for the repair, `repair_hours`. The switched share is the same for both customer classes. Customers come in two classes: `residential` customers cost `residential_cost` ($k per customer-hour) and `critical` ones (clinics, water pumping) cost `critical_cost`. The crew and parts cost `repair_cost` ($k).

items: `consequence(f)`: the cost of one failure of feeder `f`, in $k;
`saidi_minutes(f, customers_served)`: how many minutes one failure adds to the company's SAIDI, where `customers_served` is every customer of the company.

blocks.text: Write each as a formula first: the average hours a customer of this feeder is out, then the interruption cost of each class, then the sum. With $`s`$ the switched share, the average hours out are $`s \cdot \text{switch\_hours} + (1 - s) \cdot \text{repair\_hours}`$: the switched customers wait for the switching, the others for the repair. Lesson 7.3.3 has the one-class, one-step version. About eight lines.

cases.says: with one customer class and no switching, the consequence is the repair plus customers times hours times the hourly cost
critical customers are priced at their own cost per hour
the share of customers switched to another feeder is out only until the switching is done
the SAIDI contribution is customer-minutes divided by all customers served

origin.section: Consequence Is the Cost of One Failure, Added Up From Its Parts

concepts: the consequence of a failure is a sum of repair, interruption, safety and environmental parts
